title: SimpleFold: Folding Proteins via Generative Flow Matching
one_liner: Instead of hand-crafted protein folding machines, use a standard transformer trained to gradually denoise random atomic positions into real structures.
lead: Protein folding is the problem of predicting where every atom in a protein ends up in 3D space. Older folding models use expensive specialized blocks designed just for proteins. SimpleFold asks: what if we used the same general building blocks that work for language and images (standard transformers: stacked layers where each layer attends to context), and trained it like a generative model to refine noisy atom positions into real structures? This simpler approach works just as well.

problem.h2: The protein folding problem and the complexity trap
paras: A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific 3D shape. Knowing that shape tells us what the protein does — it determines whether it can bind to drugs, catalyze reactions, or break down waste. The problem: given just the sequence of amino acids, predict the 3D coordinates of every atom.

Today's best folding models use specialized architectural pieces designed specifically for proteins. They use expensive operations like triangular updates (special geometric tricks), explicit pair representations (matrices tracking which amino acids are close to each other), and multiple training objectives (different loss functions for different parts of the structure). This assumes that protein folding is so different from other problems that you need custom machinery.

A beginner would naively try: feed the sequence through a standard language model and decode the coordinates. This breaks because the model has no way to maintain 3D geometric consistency—atoms would float into impossible positions, bond lengths would be wrong, and atoms would pass through each other.

callout.b: The question: Do we really need all that complexity?
callout.html: SimpleFold builds a protein folder from standard transformer blocks trained as a generative model, with no geometric machinery or domain-specific tricks.

steps.text: Sample random positions for every atom in the protein.
Pass the amino acid sequence through a transformer to build a context.
At each step, feed noisy atoms and time into a transformer; it predicts a nudge toward clean positions.
Apply the predicted movement to get slightly-less-noisy atom positions.
After many steps, atoms settle into realistic 3D coordinates.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the architecture
paras: SimpleFold replaces the entire specialized stack—triangular updates, pair representations, domain-specific modules—with a single, repeating idea: standard transformer blocks. Every part of the model (atom encoder, sequence processing, structure decoder) is built from the same general-purpose blocks, just like those that work for language translation or image generation.
object.object: The architecture: from specialized to standard

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: velocity of atoms through noise
hidden.name: Predicted velocity field
paras: Central to SimpleFold is a quantity the model learns to predict but never explicitly measures: the velocity—the direction and magnitude each atom should move in the next instant. It is not a distance or a final coordinate. It is a tiny, momentary nudge calculated by the transformer at each step. The model predicts this velocity by comparing noisy atom positions and the amino acid sequence.

The paper trains the model by giving it noisy atomic coordinates and asking it to predict the correct velocity. During training, it compares the predicted velocity to the true velocity that would move the noisy structure toward the real structure. Over billions of examples, the transformer learns to predict accurate velocities, which means that when you apply these velocities step by step, noisy atoms gradually converge to realistic positions.

heat.caption: Darker atoms need larger predicted nudges; light atoms need smaller ones or are already close.

reads.html: The velocity is the predicted movement for each atom at each step—how far to push it toward the real structure.

The network learns a velocity field by computing average error between predicted and true velocities, where the network takes as input noisy atoms, the sequence, and the time step, and outputs predicted velocities for all atoms.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: generative denoising tailored to 3D
paras: Flow matching is a generative technique: start with noise, predict the direction to move toward clean data, apply that movement repeatedly. It works for images (remove blur, add detail) and text (remove scrambling, add grammar). SimpleFold applies the same idea to atomic coordinates.

Instead of hand-tuning specialized modules to respect protein chemistry, the transformer learns it directly from data. During training, the model sees millions of real protein structures and learns what realistic configurations look like. When it predicts velocities, it learns to move atoms toward bond lengths and angles that actually exist in nature. The sequence acts as a guide—the transformer conditions on amino acids, so it learns that a cysteine prefers certain neighbors, or that a helix has predictable 3D shapes. All of this emerges from the data without explicit rules.

The additional structural loss (LDDT loss) tells the model to prioritize getting local distances right—the distance between nearby atoms. This acts as a soft constraint: it nudges the model to favor realistic pairwise distances. It does not forbid impossible structures; it just makes them less likely during training. The transformer learns which velocities produce valid structures most often.

stages.s: Amino acid sequence + noisy atom positions
Encode sequence and atoms via transformer
Predict velocity field: which way each atom should move
Apply velocities: nudge atoms closer to real positions
Repeat with less noisy atoms and different time step

math.h2: The training objective: velocity matching plus structure quality
math.words: Total loss = (velocity matching loss) + (weight depending on time) * (local distance quality loss)
math.equation:
loss = l_FM + alpha(t) * l_LDDT
l_FM = E[|| v_theta(x_t, s, t) - v_t ||^2]
symbols: the main loss: how well predicted velocity matches true velocity
predicted velocity from the transformer, given noisy atoms x_t, sequence s, and time t
the true velocity that would move x_t toward real structure
local distance difference test: penalizes getting local atom distances wrong
weighting factor that changes based on the time step, higher later in training

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine one atom at noisy position (5.2, 3.1, 1.8) that should end up at (5.5, 3.0, 2.0).
True velocity: move (0.3, -0.1, 0.2) to get closer each step.
If alpha(t) = 0.5 and l_LDDT = 0.01 for this atom, total loss = 0.0009 + 0.5*0.01 = 0.0059.
The model learns to make its velocity predictions smaller errors so loss shrinks over training.

math.note: The model minimizes the total error across all atoms. Velocity matching teaches it the direction to move; the LDDT term teaches it to prioritize realistic local structures.

charts.title: Older domain-specific models
charts.note: Domain-specific tricks minimize a single target (one best structure), so they produce one deterministic answer. When you run them multiple times they give the same result, making ensemble voting weak. Many proteins have multiple plausible folds, but these models cannot express that.

charts.title: SimpleFold (3B params)
charts.note: Flow-matching learns the spread of plausible structures (which ones are likely) by predicting velocity at each refinement step. Small random changes early in the process lead to different final structures, all realistic. This lets you run the model multiple times and get diverse predictions, so ensemble voting works well on hard cases.

items.b: Velocity training diverges if time-steps are uniform.
items.html: Early timesteps (very noisy atoms) and late timesteps (nearly clean atoms) have very different velocity magnitudes. Sampling timesteps uniformly means the model trains poorly on important fine-detail steps. SimpleFold fixes this by resampling timestamps to favor late times (closer to clean data) where details matter most.

items.b: Locality constraints are necessary to avoid computational explosion.
items.html: In a transformer (stacked layers where each layer connects pairs of items), a full all-to-all connection over every atom would multiply the compute cost with protein size. SimpleFold constrains each atom to only see nearby atoms in the sequence, keeping compute linear.

Protein structures can be rotated arbitrarily. A deterministic regression model has to pick one rotation, which is wasteful and hurts ensemble predictions. Flow matching embraces this: the model learns many plausible rotations from data and can predict an ensemble naturally.

items.b: Done right: standard transformer architecture generalizes.
items.html: Using the same blocks as language and vision models means SimpleFold can benefit from advances in transformer efficiency and scale—it is not locked into specialized 3D-only code.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny SimpleFold on a small protein (100 amino acids). Train it on distilled structures for a few iterations. The demo should show: (1) Start with uniformly random atom positions. (2) Run the model for 50 timesteps, collecting predictions at each step. (3) Overlay the predicted structure against the real structure and measure RMSD (root mean square deviation—average displacement of atoms in Angstroms). The curve should show RMSD dropping from ~15 Angstroms (complete noise) to ~2-3 Angstroms (near-realistic) as refinement steps accumulate.
demo.metric_eq: RMSD at step t = sqrt(mean((predicted_pos - real_pos)^2)) for all atoms
demo.closing: The core proof: a standard transformer, trained only to predict velocity and local distance quality, can refine random atoms into protein-like structures. No specialized layers needed.
